title: FRM Current Issues, Lesson 3: Stablecoins and systemic risk from digital assets
subtitle: A token that promises a "1:1 peg" can still lose that peg within hours - and take a whole ecosystem down with it
whyItMatters: Stablecoins have grown into a significant part of the digital asset payment system, with a combined market capitalisation in the hundreds of billions of dollars. But their promise of being "stable 1:1 with the USD" rests on very different mechanisms - some fully backed by reserve assets, some driven by an algorithm with no real collateral behind it - and the collapse of the second kind has become the classic case study of current issues in the FRM.
openingQuestion: What is the core difference between an asset-backed stablecoin and an algorithmic one?
openingOptions: There is no difference at all; both carry the same level of risk and are governed by the same technical mechanism
Asset-backed coins hold real reserves; algorithmic ones do not
Algorithmic stablecoins are always safer because they depend on no traditional financial institution whatsoever
Asset-backed stablecoins exist only in theory and have never actually been issued on any real market
explanation: Asset-backed stablecoins such as USDC and USDT claim to hold reserves equal in value to the tokens in circulation, though the quality and transparency of those reserves varies a great deal between issuers. Algorithmic stablecoins such as TerraUSD (UST) before its collapse hold no equivalent reserve at all; they defend the peg through an arbitrage mechanism between the main token and a companion token - a mechanism that only works while market confidence is intact.

diagram.label: An algorithmic stablecoin holds its peg through arbitrage with a companion token
Market confidence weakens and investors begin to sell out
Arbitrage cannot absorb the selling pressure and the peg breaks (de-peg)
A self-reinforcing downward spiral - main token and companion token collapse together

realWorldExample.description: UST held its 1 USD peg through a two-way swap with the Luna token: 1 UST could always be exchanged for 1 USD worth of Luna and vice versa. When a large volume of UST was sold all at once, arbitrage could not absorb it and UST slipped off the peg. The two-way swap meant that "defending" the peg required minting Luna at extraordinary speed, so Luna's supply exploded and its price collapsed to near zero within days, wiping out roughly 40bn USD of market value across the whole ecosystem.

quiz.question: Why did the two-way swap between UST and Luna turn into a self-destroying spiral once confidence broke?
options: Because the interest rate paid on UST deposits was cut abruptly
Because the reserve fund's Bitcoin holdings had already been spent down
Because exchanges all halted UST withdrawals for several days
Because defending the peg meant minting more Luna, sinking its price
quiz.explanation: This is a textbook self-reinforcing feedback loop: the mechanism designed to stabilise the price becomes the amplifier of the crisis once selling pressure passes a certain threshold - no different in kind from leverage amplifying losses, which you met back in the Foundations stage. The yield cut and the reserve sales were consequences along the way, and the exchange halts came after the peg had already gone.

quiz.question: Why is an asset-backed stablecoin - one backed by Treasury bills, say - still not fully immune to losing its peg?
options: Reserve quality and liquidity can differ from what is disclosed
Because US Treasury bonds are inherently high default-risk assets
Because this type of stablecoin is not permitted to audit its reserves
Because reserve assets always have to be sold at a loss on redemption
quiz.explanation: This connects straight back to the Liquidity and Treasury Risk stage: if the backing reserves are not liquid enough to meet a simultaneous wave of redemptions - even where their stated value is sufficient - or if the audit of those reserves is not credible, the coin can still break its peg in a run. Treasuries are among the lowest-default-risk assets there are, audits are routine rather than forbidden, and reserves held to maturity need not be sold at a loss at all.

quiz.question: Why do financial regulators treat systemic risk from stablecoins as a "current issue" worth close monitoring, even though the sector is far smaller than the traditional banking system?
options: Because stablecoin size has now passed the banking industry's total assets
Because their links to the traditional financial system are growing fast
Because stablecoins sit outside every existing legal framework today
Because every stablecoin shares one single issuing institution
quiz.explanation: This is exactly the interconnection pattern from the previous lesson: absolute size is not the only determinant of systemic risk - the degree of connection matters at least as much. Several large stablecoins hold substantial amounts of US Treasury bills as reserves, so a mass run out of a stablecoin could force Treasury sales that feed straight back into traditional markets.

quiz.question: What general lesson from the TerraUSD/Luna collapse maps onto the failure pattern learned in Foundations of Risk Management (LTCM, the 2008 crisis)?
options: A mechanism that works in calm markets amplifies the shock in a crisis
Both stemmed from deliberate fraud committed by the management team
Both were flagged in advance by regulators and the warnings ignored
Both collapsed because leverage exceeded the legal limits allowed
quiz.explanation: This is the thread running through the whole FRM path: whether it is LTCM's leverage, the tranching of CDOs, or the UST/Luna two-way swap, the failure pattern is always the same - a mechanism that stabilises things under normal conditions turns into the amplifier of the crisis at precisely the moment it was most expected to help.

quiz.question: Why can a stablecoin backed by real assets still lose its peg?
options: Because new issuance dilutes the value of the tokens already circulating
Because the issuer is not allowed to hold short-dated Treasury bills
Because the reserve assets are revalued at the daily exchange rate
Because reserves must be dumped to meet redemptions, and dumping loses
quiz.explanation: This is exactly the mechanics of a bank run in a different wrapper: the reserves are real but they are not instant cash, while the holders all redeem at the same time. USDC lost its peg in March 2023 because part of its reserves was stranded at a bank that had just been closed.

practicePrompt.question: A stablecoin discloses reserves that are 100% short-dated corporate commercial paper, audited quarterly. Is there still de-peg risk?
options: Yes: redemption is daily while the reserves cannot be sold on demand
No: 100% reserves guarantee every coin always redeems at par value
No: a quarterly audit already rules out any shortfall in the reserves
Yes, but only if the issuer is deliberately lying about its reserves
practicePrompt.explanation: Reserves that are 100% funded and reserves that are SELLABLE TODAY are two different things - which is precisely the bank-run problem in familiar clothing. Holders can redeem daily, while corporate commercial paper can lose its liquidity in a stress episode at exactly the moment it needs to be sold, and a hurried sale goes below par. At that point the reserve ratio on paper is still 100% while the coin's market price is already below 1. A quarterly audit only photographs one moment and speaks to sufficiency, not to the quality and liquidity of the assets on the worst day.

keyTakeaways: Asset-backed stablecoins are supported by auditable reserve assets; algorithmic ones rely on a supply-and-demand mechanism with no equivalent collateral
TerraUSD/Luna (May 2022): a two-way swap designed to protect the peg became a self-destroying spiral once selling pressure crossed a threshold, wiping out roughly 40bn USD
Even asset-backed stablecoins are not immune to de-peg risk if reserve quality, reserve liquidity or audit transparency fall short
Growing links between digital assets and traditional finance (through Treasury reserves) make stablecoin risk a current issue even at a size well below the banking system

summary.keyIdea: The main risk in a stablecoin is not the technology but the quality of the reserves and the ability to redeem - which is the classic bank-run problem in a new wrapper.
summary.commonMistake: Treating a collateral-backed stablecoin as absolutely safe. It still breaks its peg if the reserves are illiquid at the moment everyone redeems at once.

application.title: Where it joins traditional finance
application.message: Stablecoin reserves sit largely in short-dated Treasury bills. A large redemption wave therefore becomes a large bond sale - and the risk stops staying inside the digital asset world.

sections.text: This is the last lesson of this FRM expansion, and it closes the circle: the failure pattern from the very first lesson of the Foundations stage - a stabilising mechanism turning into an amplifier of crisis - repeats itself exactly inside a technology less than a decade old.
Two ways to hold a peg, two different kinds of risk

left.label: Asset-backed stablecoin
left.text: Backed by reserve assets (cash, Treasury bills) - the risk sits in the quality, the liquidity and the audit transparency of those reserves.

right.label: Algorithmic stablecoin
right.text: Holds no equivalent reserve; the peg is defended by a supply-and-demand arbitrage mechanism with a companion token - the risk sits in that mechanism itself once confidence collapses.

sections.label: Why this is still a "current issue" rather than a closed one
sections.text: After the UST/Luna collapse, most purely algorithmic stablecoins lost the market's confidence, but the digital asset ecosystem kept developing new mechanisms - hybrid coins, partly backed by real assets and partly by an algorithm. The structure of the risk always changes faster than regulators can issue new rules, which is the defining feature of every topic in Current Issues in Financial Markets.

lines: From ERM in the first lesson of Foundations to stablecoins here: the technology keeps changing, but the question a risk manager has to ask stays the same - what does this mechanism assume, and does that assumption still hold when everything goes wrong at once.
This is the final lesson of this round of the FRM path expansion.
